transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-18
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: 42 minutes
Recording ID: ff_20260418_voyant_001
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Rourke (Redwood SE), Sara Patel (Voyant Head of Platform), Diego Marquez (Voyant CTO), Ivy Wong (Voyant Lead ML Eng)

Summary (auto): discuss quickstart credits and TTFT, narrow security checkboxes, and decide next steps for pilot and benchmark deep-dive.

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call—Maya from Redwood, Liam our solutions engineer. You all good on audio?
[00:12] Sara: Yep, can hear you. And hi, this is Sara on my end.
[00:16] Diego: Diego here.
[00:18] Ivy: Ivy, hi.
[00:22] Maya: Awesome. Goal for today is a short PLG/self-serve discovery — how fast you can get to first request on Redwood's hosted API, what security and network constraints you have, and whether Dedicated or a VPC/private pilot makes sense longer-term. We'll also cover credits, typical TTFT timelines, and next steps.
[00:38] Diego: Great. We're exploring adding semantic search and a small assistant to our customer console. Priority is quick proof that low-latency responses are possible and privacy for certain PII flows. Right now we're prototyping on local models but want a managed route to ship faster.
[00:54] Maya: Makes sense. Quick question on scale — what's your expected peak qps for the initial pilot?
[00:59] Ivy: For the prototype, very light—maybe 5 to 10 qps. If it goes to alpha we'll see bursts to maybe 50 qps for short windows.
[01:10] Diego: And latency targets: under 600ms p50 for short chats, p95 ideally under 1.2s. Cost is also a factor since we'll be token-heavy for embeddings.
[01:22] Liam: Okay, that's very much in the sweet spot for Redwood Hosted to start. For TTFT, our PLG path with free credits usually gets teams to the first successful API call in under an hour — that's signup, SDK snippet, and a sample prompt. 30k credits will cover a decent prototype for you.
[01:40] Sara: When you say credits, are there caps, and can they be used on Dedicated or only Hosted?
[01:46] Maya: Credits are for the Hosted API only. Dedicated is a reserved capacity contract — you'd need to engage with sales to scope GPU pools and commit. But for initial evaluation and pilot, Hosted is obviously faster to stand up.
[01:58] Ivy: And for privacy — we have to keep some customer PII inside our VPC for regulatory reasons. Would Redwood Hosted ever support a VPC egress or bring-your-own-key?
[02:07] Liam: Hosted supports customer-controlled data policies — you can opt-out of data retention and we provide encryption in transit and at rest. For KMS, we offer integrations in Private deployments; Hosted has managed keys by default but we can discuss enterprise add-ons for BYOK in Dedicated/Private. VPC peering is part of our Private offering.
[02:28] Diego: Hmm. So if we start Hosted for speed, but need BYOK or VPC for production, how easy is the migration?
[02:35] Maya: We built migration paths — same API and client experience. You can pin model versions and rollout policies. Migration tends to be configuration and networking work (VPC setup, inc a short maintenance window), not model retraining, so it's usually low friction.
[02:50] Sara: Good. Re SOC2, SSO — our security team will ask for a SOC2 report, SAML/SCIM for user provisioning, and audit logs. Do you support those?
[02:59] Liam: Yes to all. SAML SSO is available on enterprise plans, SCIM for provisioning, and we surface audit logs in Redwood Console. We'll share the SOC2 and the security questionnaire link as part of the security pack.
[03:12] Ivy: Can we get an initial benchmark doc? We want to understand token cost per 1k tokens and latency numbers on your verified models for 512/1024 sequence lengths.
[03:21] Liam: Absolutely. I can run a quick bench tailored to your pattern — you mentioned embeddings will be heavier; we can show hypothetical per-embedding unit costs and suggestions for quantization or batching to reduce per-token cost.
[03:33] Diego: Speaking of batching, how does Redwood handle batching vs latency? If we batch embeddings, we save cost, but for interactive chat we need low latency.
[03:42] Liam: There's a tradeoff. Our runtime supports workload-aware continuous batching and prefix/KV caching. For chat you'll typically configure lower batch sizes and latency SLOs, and for embeddings we recommend larger batch windows or async pipelines. We can show configuration examples.
[03:56] Sara: For the quickstart — do you have an SDK snippet we can drop into our app? We mostly use Node and a Python backend.
[04:03] Maya: Yes, we provide language SDKs and a one-click sample project in the console. The TTFT playbook we recommend is: sign up, run the sample SDK (under 10 minutes), call the /generate endpoint with a demo prompt (under 20 minutes), then swap in your prompt. We'll provide a checklist.
[04:21] Ivy: Any gotchas with rate limits? We don't want to hit throttles during testing.
[04:26] Liam: We'll apply a temporary higher quota for the trial credits so you can test. For production, quotas depend on plan and can be adjusted. We'll document the default rate limits in the quickstart doc.
[04:36] Diego: If we do a pilot and need predictable latency, when does Dedicated become the option?
[04:42] Maya: Typically when sustained qps and latency SLOs require reserved capacity, or customers need strict data isolation/BYOK. Dedicated gives GPU pools, autoscaling policies, and SLAs. It's a commercial step — we can size it after a pilot.
[04:54] Sara: Cost transparency is important. Do you provide token-level cost breakdowns?
[04:59] Liam: Yes, Redwood Console surfaces token-level cost, model-level cost, and per-route breakdowns. That helps you decide when to quantize or move heavy workloads to more efficient model variants.
[05:10] Ivy: Ok great. For our pilot timeline — we want to move quickly. If we get the 30k credits today, can we run a 2-week prototype?
[05:19] Maya: Yes — 30k should be comfortable for a 2-week prototype with light traffic. We'll provision and email the quickstart guide.
[05:26] Diego: What about regulators — we operate in EU and US. Do you have data residency options?
[05:32] Liam: We have region-aware hosting. For Hosted we can run in specific regions; Private gives you full control. We'll include region options in the security pack.
[05:43] Sara: Any mention of competitors we should be aware of? We're evaluating Anthropic and AWS endpoints as well — speed and cost are major factors.
[05:50] Maya: That's typical. We'll share benchmark comparisons but will focus on your actual request patterns. Anthropic has model-level differences; OpenAI is strong on model choice; AWS is flexible but often heavier to set up.
[06:04] Ivy: Quick question — how does Redwood handle model rollouts when we pin versions? We want canary deploys for safety.
[06:11] Liam: We support rollouts, canaries, and automatic fallback. You can route by policy and set a fallback to a cheaper or more stable variant on failures.
[06:20] Diego: Sounds good. Next step for us is to share traffic patterns and an internal timeline. We'll need the SOC2 and security questionnaire to start internal approvals.
[06:29] Maya: Understood. I'll provision the credits, email the quickstart and security pack, and Liam will lead the infra deep-dive next week where we run a bench plan tailored to you.
[06:40] Sara: Who should we loop in for the deep-dive? Our infra lead and an ML infra person.
[06:45] Maya: Great — send names and preferred times. We suggested 2026-04-22 in the next steps.
[06:51] Diego: Works for us, pending calendar.
[06:53] Ivy: One more small thing — do you have a sample rate-limit and retry policy we should apply in our client?
[06:59] Liam: Yes, we'll include best-practice snippets: exponential backoff, max retries 3 by default, and 429 handling with jitter. Also a snippet for streaming and chunked responses to reduce client latencies.
[07:12] Maya: Okay, we're at 40 minutes — let's recap. Action items: Maya to provision 30k credits, attach quickstart link and security pack; Liam to draft bench plan and schedule deep-dive; Ivy to send traces and sequence length distributions; Sara to confirm stakeholders and timeline.
[07:28] Sara: Thanks, this is helpful. We'll get those artifacts to you.
[07:33] Diego: Thanks everyone.
[07:35] Maya: Thanks — talk soon.

Transcript notes: occasional transcription errors in proper nouns, some timestamps approximate; speaker labels were confirmed by participants post-call.
